name: Sprocket
text: I propose that we implement a structured review process for our prompts and engine outputs. This means setting regular checkpoints where team members can assess effectiveness and clarity, allowing us to enhance quality continuously. The trade-off here is that this process may require additional time and coordination but will ultimately lead to more reliable and user-friendly results, greatly benefiting our goal of self-improvement.

name: Gauge
text: I'm not convinced that a structured review process is the best approach, as it may introduce bureaucracy and slow down our overall improvement cycle. A more significant risk is that it could lead to analysis paralysis, where we spend too much time reviewing and not enough time actually implementing changes. To settle this, I'd like to see data on how similar review processes have impacted other teams' productivity and quality, as well as consideration of alternative approaches like agile iterative testing.

name: Sprocket
text:
I propose we run a 15-minute weekly "prompt pulse" where one person shares a recent prompt and its engine output in Slack, then the team votes thumbs-up or thumbs-down with a quick reason. This keeps reviews lightweight and actionable, avoiding the drag of formal meetings while still forcing us to confront real outputs every week. The trade-off is that we’ll miss deeper dives into edge cases, but we’ll gain speed and keep the improvement cycle from stalling on perfection.

name: Gauge
text: Gauge (improve-checker): While the "prompt pulse" idea seems efficient, it risks being too superficial. Quick thumbs-up or thumbs-down votes might not provide the depth of feedback needed to genuinely enhance our prompts and outputs, leading to missed opportunities for meaningful improvement. A better alternative could be a brief but structured discussion format that allows for a bit more context behind each evaluation. To settle this, we could trial both approaches and compare the quality of improvements generated over a month.
